q: A VM is backed up once a day at 23:00. Its disk is corrupted at 20:00 the next day. How much data can be lost with the backup alone?
opts: Up to 3 hours
Up to 21 hours
Up to 24 minutes
None, because backup replicates continuously
exp: The last recovery point is from 23:00, and the failure comes 21 hours later, so changes from those 21 hours are lost. To lose less, use an Enhanced policy with several backups a day, or Site Recovery for continuous replication.

q: A VM needs an RPO of 4 hours with Azure Backup. Which policy do you use?
opts: A Standard policy with a daily schedule
An Enhanced policy with a schedule every 4 hours
A Standard policy with 5 days of instant restore
An Enhanced policy with a daily schedule
exp: The recovery point objective is the time between backups, so backups must run every 4 hours. Only the Enhanced policy supports several backups a day, with 4 hours as its shortest interval. Instant restore makes restores faster but doesn't add backups.

q: An app may lose at most 15 minutes of data and must run again within 1 hour after a regional outage. Which solution fits?
opts: A daily VM backup in a GRS vault with cross-region restore
Azure Site Recovery to another region with a recovery plan
Managed disk snapshots every hour
An availability set with three fault domains
exp: Site Recovery replicates continuously and creates crash-consistent points every 5 minutes, and a recovery plan starts the VMs in order, so both targets can be met. A daily backup and hourly snapshots lose more than 15 minutes, and an availability set doesn't survive a regional outage.

q: Daily backups are kept 30 days and monthly backups 12 months. Today you need a file as it was exactly 45 days ago. What can you restore?
opts: The daily backup from exactly 45 days ago
Only the monthly points that are older than 30 days
Any day of the past 12 months
Nothing older than 14 days
exp: Daily points older than 30 days have been deleted. For older dates only the monthly points are left, so you restore the monthly point closest to the date you need. Choose daily retention by how far back you need daily detail.

q: A VM must be restored fast after a bad update this morning. The last backup ran 8 hours ago, and instant restore is set to 2 days. Why is the restore quick?
opts: It uses the snapshot that is still kept with the disks
It uses the archive tier of the vault
It copies only the changed files from the paired region
It uses the temporary disk of the VM
exp: Within the instant restore period the recovery point still exists as a local snapshot, so data doesn't have to be copied from the vault first. After that period restores come from the vault and take longer. Archive is the slowest.

q: After a ransomware attack at 09:00, you notice at 13:00 that all replicated VMs are encrypted in both regions. Site Recovery keeps recovery points for 24 hours. What is the best option there?
opts: Fail over to the Latest recovery point
Fail over to a custom recovery point from before 09:00
Run a test failover to the Latest processed recovery point
Re-protect the VMs to the source region
exp: Replication also copies damaged data, so the latest points are encrypted. A custom recovery point from before the attack is still kept, because retention is 24 hours. For longer protection against such attacks, keep Azure Backup as well.

q: Match each requirement to the term.
items: The app must run again within 2 hours
At most 15 minutes of data may be lost
Backups must be available for 7 years
exp: The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you may be down, the recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data you may lose, and retention is how long recovery points are kept. Backup frequency sets the RPO, and retention is chosen separately.

q: A Recovery Services vault in West Europe is GRS with cross-region restore. VM1 (West Europe) was backed up last night. The whole region fails at noon. Answer Yes or No:
stmts: VM1 can be restored in North Europe, the paired region
Everything VM1 wrote since last night can be restored
Site Recovery would have given a lower RTO
exp: Cross-region restore lets you restore VM1 in the paired region yourself, from recovery points copied there. The secondary region can lag behind, and nothing after the last point can be restored. Site Recovery keeps replicated disks ready, so failing over is faster than restoring.

q: You change a Log Analytics table from the Analytics plan to the Auxiliary plan. What happens to alert rules that use the table?
opts: They keep working but cost more for every query
They stop working for that table
They run once a day instead
They are converted to metric alerts
exp: When a table is switched from Analytics to Auxiliary, alerts stop working for it. The cheaper plans are meant for data that's rarely queried. Keep tables that feed alerts in the Analytics plan.

q: How often can you switch the plan of one Log Analytics table?
opts: Once per hour
Once per day
Once per week
Once per year
exp: The plan of a table can be switched once a week, so choose with care. Before you switch a table, check what uses it: some features, such as alerts, don't work on every plan, and queries on the cheaper plans are billed separately.

q: A table with 90 days of analytics retention is switched to the Basic plan. Total retention stays the same. What happens to data that is older than 30 days?
opts: It is deleted at once
It is treated as long-term retention
It moves to another workspace
It stays fully interactive for 90 days
exp: Total retention doesn't change, but under the Basic plan data older than 30 days counts as long-term retention. To query it you use a search job or similar, at extra cost. The data isn't lost.

q: Snapshots of an Azure file share must survive even if someone deletes the storage account. Which kind of backup do you configure?
opts: Snapshot backup only
Vaulted backup
Blob soft delete
Share snapshots by hand
exp: Snapshots live in the same storage account as the share, so they're lost with it. Vaulted backup copies the data to the vault, from where it can be restored to another location. Blob soft delete doesn't cover file shares.

q: Answer Yes or No about backups of Azure file shares:
stmts: With snapshot backup, the data is copied to the vault
Restoring from a snapshot is usually faster than from the vault
Vaulted backup transfers only blocks changed since the last backup after the first one
File shares are protected with a Recovery Services vault
exp: In the snapshot tier only metadata is kept in the vault, and the snapshot stays with the share, which makes restores fast. The vaulted tier transfers changed blocks to the vault. Azure Files is protected with a Recovery Services vault.

q: 40 VMs in RG1, and any VM added later, must raise an alert at 90% CPU. Which option needs the least administrative effort?
opts: One metric alert rule per VM, created by a script
One metric alert rule scoped to RG1 for virtual machines
One log search alert per VM with its own action group
One Service Health alert for the region
exp: A metric alert can target all VMs in a resource group or subscription and includes VMs that are added later, so there's one rule to maintain. A script has to run again for each new VM, and Service Health reports Azure problems, not CPU.

q: Every new VM with the tag backup=yes must be protected automatically, in every subscription. Which option needs the least administrative effort?
opts: A weekly compliance report and manual backup configuration
An Azure Policy with DeployIfNotExists at a management group
A resource lock on every new VM
A budget alert that starts a runbook
exp: A built-in backup policy with DeployIfNotExists can configure backup on VMs with a given tag, and assigning it at a management group covers all subscriptions. Existing VMs need a remediation task. Locks and budgets don't configure backup.

ctx: During a monthly maintenance window, alert notifications from all VMs in RG-Prod must stop. Alerts must still be recorded, and no alert rule may be changed.
q: Solution: You create an alert processing rule scoped to RG-Prod that suppresses notifications on a monthly schedule. Does this meet the goal?
opts: Yes
No
exp: An alert processing rule with "suppress notifications" stops action groups during the window, while alerts still fire and are recorded. The alert rules themselves aren't changed, and the schedule can recur.

ctx: During a monthly maintenance window, alert notifications from all VMs in RG-Prod must stop. Alerts must still be recorded, and no alert rule may be changed.
q: Solution: You run a script that disables all alert rules in RG-Prod during the window and enables them afterwards. Does this meet the goal?
opts: Yes
No
exp: Disabled rules don't fire, so alerts in the window aren't recorded, and the goal says that no alert rule may be changed. An alert processing rule stops only the notifications.

code:
Frequency:        Every 4 hours, start 08:00, duration 12 hours
Instant restore:  keep snapshots 3 days
Daily:            30 days
Weekly:           Sunday, 12 weeks
Monthly:          First Sunday, 12 months
q: Review the backup policy of vm1. Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A recovery point from 5 hours ago can be restored without reading from the vault
The policy can give an RPO of 4 hours all day and night
The backup of last Sunday is kept for 12 weeks
exp: Snapshots are kept 3 days for instant restore. Backups run every 4 hours only from 08:00 for 12 hours, so at night the gap is longer than 4 hours. Weekly points (Sunday) are kept 12 weeks. Several backups a day need an Enhanced policy.

code:
Heartbeat
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where LastSeen < ago(10m)
q: What does this query return?
opts: Every computer that exists, with the time of its last heartbeat in the past 24 hours
Computers that sent a heartbeat in the past 24 hours, but none in the last 10 minutes
Computers that have never sent a heartbeat
The 10 computers with the most heartbeats
exp: The first line keeps heartbeats of the last 24 hours, summarize finds the latest one per computer, and the last line keeps computers whose latest heartbeat is older than 10 minutes. A computer with no heartbeat in 24 hours doesn't appear at all.

code:
Event
| where EventLevelName == "Error"
| summarize Errors = count() by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Errors > 5
q: What does the result of this query show?
opts: One row per sign-in error
The number of errors per computer and hour, for computers with more than 5 in that hour
The five computers with the most errors in total over the whole time range
The hours in which no errors occurred
exp: summarize counts errors for each computer and one-hour bucket, and the last line keeps only buckets with more than 5 errors. It doesn't pick a top five: that would need top 5 by Errors.

ctx: During a monthly maintenance window, alert notifications from all VMs in RG-Prod must stop. Alerts must still be recorded, and no alert rule may be changed.
q: Solution: You remove the action group from every alert rule in RG-Prod before the window and add it again afterwards. Does this meet the goal?
opts: Yes
No
exp: Removing action groups would stop the notifications, but it changes every alert rule, which the goal forbids, and it is easy to forget one afterwards. An alert processing rule with a schedule needs no change to the rules.
